w: Built between 1947 and 1950 on the model of Paris's Longchamp Racecourse, this 47-hectare track by the Sava has hosted the June Tournament every year since 1955 and stables around 160 horses. Its strangest chapter: in 1994, Pope John Paul II said mass here to a crowd of a million - Pope Benedict XVI followed in 2011.
s: Croatia's Longchamp, and once a papal altar
_facts: Built 1947-1950, design based on Longchamp Racecourse in Paris
Covers 47 hectares in Kajzerica, near Bundek lake
Annual International June Tournament held since 1955; stables hold around 160 horses
Pope John Paul II celebrated mass here in 1994 attended by a million people; Pope Benedict XVI in 2011

n: Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts
w: Founded in 1866 under Bishop Josip Juraj Strossmayer's patronage, this started life as the Yugoslav Academy of Sciences and Arts - its founder wanted a central scientific and artistic hub for all South Slavs. It began with 16 full members; today it counts around 160, across nine classes from mathematics to fine arts.
s: Croatia's national academy, founded by a bishop
_facts: Founded 1866 under patronage of Bishop Josip Juraj Strossmayer as the Yugoslav Academy of Sciences and Arts
Started with 16 full members, grown to about 160 today
Divided into nine classes covering social sciences through fine and musical arts

w: Croatia's first luxury hotel opened in 1925 for one specific clientele: passengers stepping off the Orient Express on its run between Paris and Istanbul. It's stood on Starcevic Square ever since, one of Zagreb's defining landmarks and a rare surviving thread to the golden age of continental rail travel.
s: Built in 1925 for Orient Express passengers
_facts: Built in 1925 to accommodate Orient Express passengers
First luxury hotel in Croatia
Located on Starcevic Square; one of Zagreb's main landmarks

w: Established in 1898 on the Lenuci Horseshoe, this is the oldest gallery in Southeast Europe and the only one in Zagreb built specifically to host large-scale exhibitions. It sits at the edge of King Tomislav Square, facing the central station, still doing exactly the job it was built for well over a century ago.
_facts: Established 1898; art gallery on the Lenuci Horseshoe in Zagreb's Lower Town
Oldest gallery in Southeast Europe
Only purpose-built gallery in Zagreb designed specifically for large-scale exhibitions

w: Founded in 1919, this sits inside a 1903 Secession building once the Trades Hall, facade decorated by sculptor Rudolf Valdec, dome frescoed by Oton Ivekovic. The 80,000-item collection spans Croatia's Pannonian, Dinaric and Adriatic zones, with reconstructed farmhouses and rooms built around birth, life and death.
s: 80,000 objects of Croatian folk life, in a Secession shell
_facts: Founded 1919 by Salamon Berger
Housed in a 1903 Secession building, formerly a Trades Hall, designed by Vjekoslav Bastl
Facade statues by Rudolf Valdec; dome frescoes by Oton Ivekovic
Holdings of about 80,000 items covering Pannonian, Dinaric and Adriatic cultural zones; about 2,800 on display

n: Basilica of the Heart of Jesus
w: Designed by Croatian architect Janko Holjac in neo-Baroque style and dedicated to the Sacred Heart, this is Zagreb's second-largest church after the cathedral itself. The Jesuits have run it ever since it went up on Palmoticeva street, a quieter counterpart to the city's more famous spires.
s: Zagreb's second-largest church, run by the Jesuits
_facts: Roman Catholic basilica on Palmoticeva street, designed by Janko Holjac in neo-Baroque style
Dedicated to the Sacred Heart
Second largest church in Zagreb after Zagreb Cathedral; run by the Jesuits

w: This theatre opened on Frankopanska street on 30 October 1954, taking over from the 'Helios' cinema that industrialist Adolf Muller had founded and financed there. One venue's screen became another's stage - a small but telling swap in Zagreb's cultural map.
s: A theatre that grew out of a vanished cinema
_facts: Opened 30 October 1954 in Frankopanska Street
Successor to the 'Helios' cinema, founded and financed by Croatian industrialist Adolf Muller

w: Built in 1903-04 for industrialist Josip Kallina, this corner house is wrapped floor to roof in decorative ceramic tiles - all made by Kallina's own ceramics factory, turning his home into a giant advertisement. Architect Vjekoslav Bastl, trained under Otto Wagner in Vienna, added Art Nouveau florals and a bat motif.
s: A house wallpapered in its own owner's ceramic tiles
_facts: Built 1903-1904 for industrialist Josip Kallina, designed by Vjekoslav Bastl for Honigsberg & Deutsch
Entire facade covered in decorative ceramic tiles produced by Kallina's own ceramics factory
Bastl studied under Otto Wagner in Vienna; design influenced by the Majolika Haus
Features decorative iron balconies and a bat-shaped patterned motif

w: Sculptor Đuro Kavuric built this tomb in Zagreb's Mirogoj cemetery in 1968 to hold the recipients of the Order of the People's Hero alongside notable workers'-movement figures. In 2001, unknown vandals detonated an explosive in front of it - officials condemned the attack, and the damage was later repaired.
s: A war memorial that was once bombed by vandals
_facts: Located in Mirogoj cemetery, Zagreb; designed by sculptor Đuro Kavuric, built 1968
Holds recipients of the Order of the People's Hero and notable workers'-movement activists
On 1 February 2001, an explosive device damaged the tomb in an act of vandalism; later repaired
